Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 19)
Topic: Bhakti's Five Stages, and the Full Truth About Kaam Vasana

Sour ce: Bhaiya's live satsang session (video transcript, ~92 min), Mool T attva/Gyaan series. Covers what genuinely defines a "bhakt" (true devotee) versus a "sadhak" (practitioner), the five sequential stages (charan) a person cr osses on the way to becoming a bhakt, and — as the session's fourth stage — an extended, dir ect teaching on kaam vasana (sexual desir e): its natural cycle, what does and doesn't help manage it, married-couple ener gy dynamics, addiction risks (including pornography), and r elated live sangat Q&A. Purpose: Chatbot knowledge — English version. Note on r egister: this session addr esses sexual desir e dir ectly and candidly , in the same measur ed, non-graphic, non-shaming spirit as Sessions 12, 17, and 18 — practical and reassuring rather than moralizing.
1. WHO IS A BHAKT? — THE STARTING QUESTION

A bhakt (true devotee) is not simply someone who chants Ram's name, has done six months of sadhna, or performs eight hours of daily jaap. Doing these things makes someone a sadhak — a practitioner — but a bhakt is described as something much bigger and dif ferent in kind. A specific prayer used at Ashaeiynn (deliberately kept private, never published elsewhere) captur es this directly: "Main bhavuk toh hoon par nahi bhakt hoon" — "I am emotional/sentimental, but I am not (yet) a devotee." This humility is treated as the correct starting posture — Bhaiya states plainly that even he considers himself "bhavuk," not a fully realized "bhakt."
2. SADHAK VS. BHAKT — THE KEY DISTINCTION

A sadhak is "one who sadhta hai" — someone who practices: works with a mantra, performs kriya, holds an asana, and attains a siddhi as a r esult. That is sadhna — a defined, bounded activity . A bhakt is categorically larger than this. Becoming a bhakt requires crossing five sequential stages (charan) — this is described explicitly as universal truth (not "bookish knowledge"), which is why saints across traditions, despite dif fering styles, ultimately conver ge on saying the same underlying thing.
3. ST AGE ONE — CONFLICT WITH THOSE AROUND YOU

The moment a person begins genuine bhakti, the people closest to them (par ents, spouse) typically start cr eating friction — pushback, ar guments, complaints. Crossing this first stage means learning to work thr ough this friction and moving on to working on oneself.
4. ST AGE TWO — WORKING ON YOUR OWN INNER SELF

The second stage is the work of calming one's own antaratma (inner self) — recognizing one's own restlessness, inner vasana, physical discomforts during practice (not being able to sit still, aches, digestive discomfort), and the many small resistances the mind and body throw up. Crossing this stage means these inner obstacles genuinely begin to settle.
5. ST AGE THREE — RECEIVING SHAKTI (AND WHY IT'S DANGEROUS)

The third stage is r eceiving shakti (power) — and this stage is explicitly called out as very important and genuinely risky . Shakti is equated here with maya (worldly illusion/attraction): once a person receives shakti, three things are quickly drawn toward them, in modest quantities each — money (paisa), power/fame (naam-fame), and some degree of respect (izzat). These three arriving together tend to make a person feel like "I am everything." This typically happens around the time a person attains their first siddhi. The trap: at this exact stage, people (both the person themselves and others ar ound them) start declaring "I have become a bhakt." Many practitioners get permanently stuck here — pulled by the lure of money , or overtaken by pride (ghamand) in their newly acquired power . Illustrative story: a disciple who attains a siddhi thr ough six months of dedicated sadhna can become so consumed by that siddhi that they begin judging everyone ar ound them — including their own Guru — as "wr ong" or "bad," reasoning "I alone am good, because the siddhi came specifically to me." This is described precisely as "shakti ka guroor" (the pride of power) — maya re-trapping the practitioner through the very power meant to elevate them. Falling at every stage is described as inevitable and universal — no one cr osses all five stages flawlessly . The real failure is not falling; it's failing to get back up afterward ("giro toh phir uth jao" — if you fall, rise again). Those who don't rise remain stuck in stage three's repeating cycle: small gains of money or power , followed by loss, on repeat — because maya has a strict, fixed ceiling at this stage and will never give mor e than that ceiling allows, no matter what. The genuine sign of having cr ossed stage thr ee: fame, r ecognition, and pr osperity arrive on their own, entir ely unsolicited — people start seeking the practitioner out, recognizing them, calling them unprompted, wanting their guidance. This is described as an unbr eakable principle: "they will come for you." Conversely , no one can validly declare for themselves, ahead of time, "I have crossed stage three" — it's only recognizable by this unsolicited external recognition actually arriving. Explicit warning: never boast about years of jaap or self-declar e devotee status befor e this recognition genuinely arrives on its own. The instructed posture until then: work hard, keep taking God's name, strive for real completion of stage three — and refrain from "preaching" (gyaan pelna) to others until you've actually reached it yourself. A related encouragement: sincer e, hard effort in jaap can cut even one's largest sin or dosha — no single moment of practice is wasted; it all "counts." A direct promise is given: commit to this teaching for one year , sitting for roughly six hours of jaap, and by the end of that year , life circumstances will have genuinely transformed — enough that a practitioner will feel permanently grateful that Ram's name changed their fate, gave them a path, and gave them everything.
6. ST AGE FOUR — KAAM VASANA (SEXUAL DESIRE)

Clarified dir ectly in r esponse to a live question: this stage is specifically about kaam vasana (sexual desir e/attraction) — not general sensory desir e (food pr eferences, talkativeness, and similar ordinary appetites), which do NOT disqualify anyone fr om bhakti or bhakt status. Kaam vasana is tr eated with r eal seriousness — described as a genuinely massive concept that "shakes the whole world," never to be taken lightly . It is present in every human being, whether wanted or not, and it never fully "dies" in a person — even as it naturally lessens somewhat with age, it never fully disappears. A strong warning against ever declaring "I have conquer ed desire": even great rishis and munis have been trapped by proudly claiming exactly this; it is described as too big a word to safely claim for oneself. This stage is genuinely cr ossed only thr ough understanding vasana's underlying tattva (natur e) via the Guru's guidance — not through willpower or self-declared control. Once crossed, a specific tattva of Bhagwan Parshuram enters the
practitioner , and they become worthy of being called a true bhakt — in the company of figures like Tulsidas ji and Surdas ji.
7. THE NATURAL CYCLE OF DESIRE — HOW IT ACTUALLY BEHAVES OVER TIME

Every person's body follows a natural desir e cycle tied to Earth's own r otation and speed — as Earth's direction and speed shift relative to other planets, this produces unexplained internal mood shifts (sudden sadness or happiness without an obvious cause) in everyone, independent of any spiritual practice. A specific pattern is described for someone beginning a sustained practice/brahmacharya period: a noticeable ur ge (arz) tends to build on day 3, day 5, and day 7; then, from the night of day 13 through day 21, this ur ge recurs continuously — as often as five to six times a day . This pattern lessens with age but never fully disappears. If a practitioner holds thr ough day 21, an especially str ong urge/flow arrives ar ound day 29-30; r esisting that carries the practitioner directly to r oughly day 41-42. Crossing a full month brings a new stability; by day 90 (three months), a strong new baseline ener gy has formed. Longer -term pattern: after six months, a slight recurrence appears at the start of each month, but genuine control develops; after one year , hours of control become natural; after two years, practitioners typically start finding their old triggers genuinely funny rather than compelling ("is this really all it was?") — described as a real, felt shift in perception, not a performance. After roughly four years, an unusual r eversal occurs: unsolicited attraction begins happening TO the practitioner from others, without them seeking it. Their own ener gy (ojas, in this teaching's parallel usage) develops a "mohit" (captivating) quality rather than a "kheenchna" (pulling/attracting) quality — of fered as directly comparable to Bhagwan Krishna, who is described as captivating rather than actively attracting.
8. BHAIY A'S OWN TESTIMONY ON THIS JOURNEY

During college, Hanuman Ji Maharaj r epeatedly appear ed to Bhaiya in dhyana mudra in dr eams — r oughly weekly , biweekly , or monthly — even though he wasn't actively worshipping at the time. Looking back, he describes this as his Guru's grace working quietly , before he was even consciously aware of it. He had an ordinary , active college social life (including a girlfriend, and typical college socializing) through his third year , largely setting aside these signs. But whenever he specifically tried to pursue something further , circumstances would mysteriously and r epeatedly fall thr ough — described humorously as persistent "bad luck," with a specific unexpected obstacle appearing almost every time. In his third year , he had a serious partner and consider ed marriage — but the dr eams of Hanuman Ji kept intensifying, eventually leading him to take a six-month vow (pran) of full brahmacharya. His partner was initially confused, gradually coming to understand as he explained his visions and his need to pursue sadhna.
9. WHAT DOES NOT WORK — WILLPOWER AND JAAP ALONE

A direct, important corr ection: a practitioner cannot simply "contr ol" brahmacharya thr ough sheer willpower — attempting to command one's own body this way tends to backfir e sever ely , described as inviting a significant setback from every dir ection. An equally important, counterintuitive corr ection: jaap alone does NOT reduce or eliminate the underlying urge (arz) — it can actually intensify it. Both vasana (desire) and upasana (worship/practice) are described as rising together , with only a very slight dif ference between the two — heavy jaap sessions (four to six hours) can leave a practitioner feeling overwhelmed with built-up ener gy , sometimes to an uncomfortable degree, precisely because that ener gy hasn't yet been channeled elsewhere.
10. WHAT ACTUALLY HELPS

Guru sanidhya (nearness to one's Guru) is pr esented as the single most effective support. Sitting at the Guru's feet, praying sincerely and repeatedly for release from this specific vasana tattva, and genuine surrender are described as consistently bringing real relief — being physically near a saint's aura (aabhamandal) gradually clears a practitioner's own malinta (impurity). This is of fered as the deeper reason behind the old custom of visiting saints in the evening to hear bhajan, kirtan, and vaani. A saint whose own brahmacharya has r emained unbr oken for at least two years can shift others' minds simply thr ough pr oximity to their aura. When direct access to a saint/Guru isn't available, sattvic aahar (a pur e, simple diet) is highlighted as a str ong supporting factor — food genuinely af fects this dimension significantly . Moderation is the operative principle for habits like smoking or drinking: neither , on its own, "br eaks" brahmacharya, but "excess of anything cr eates toxicity in the body ," which blocks further spiritual pr ogr ess past a certain point. A cigarette or two, or moderate drinking, is treated dif ferently from consistent excess. Involuntary or circumstantially for ced brahmacharya (r epeated inability to pursue intimacy despite genuinely trying) can be r ead two ways at once: partly as simple bad luck, and partly , genuinely , as God testing the practitioner for a specific purpose.
1 1. PORNOGRAPHY AND ADDICTION

Pornography use is explicitly categorized as a form of vasana, and it r eadily becomes an addiction. It does NOT , on its own, "break" brahmacharya (since there is no physical touch and therefore no aura/ener gy exchange with another person involved) — but addiction itself "cr eates degradation," independent of the brahmacharya question specifically . The described mechanism of harm: repeated viewing habituates the practitioner to a purely visual, non-physical form of stimulation, which gradually reduces genuine satisfaction from real physical intimacy with an actual partner — described as a person's other senses ("sense of touch and presence") becoming underused and their arousal becoming disproportionately tied to sight alone. Over time this can distort how a practitioner perceives real people they encounter , generating unwanted or inappropriate thoughts. Practical guidance: work to leave this specific addiction, in God's name; having an actual real-world partner is presented as healthier than this particular addiction; if needed, redirect attention to a more constructive outlet altogether (the session's own example: adopt a pet) rather than feeding this pattern. The overarching principle stated plainly: addiction itself cr eates degradation — minimize any addiction, whatever its specific form.
12. MARRIED COUPLES — ENERGY -SHARING MECHANICS

A cor e teaching for married practitioners: don't pursue intimacy with anyone besides your own spouse — doing so does not compr omise brahmacharya in this framework. When two bodies ar e intimate, a practitioner shar es roughly half of their accumulated jaap/energy with the other person. If BOTH partners are "char ged" — actively practicing the same mantra — this exchange causes no depletion for either partner , because the ener gy in question is described as being stored in the mantra itself, not merely in the body . This is stated explicitly as a vow ("yeh vachan hai"), not a casual claim. Practical guidance when a spouse is r eluctant to chant: gently and persistently encourage them to join in the practice — even partial cooperation helps preserve both partners' ener gy , since the underlying mechanism depends on shared mantra practice. Energy given up thr ough this kind of intimate exchange can always be r ebuilt through further jaap — jaap is described as capable of restoring virtually anything in this domain.
13. NAULI KRIY A — AN ADVANCED RETENTION TECHNIQUE

Some practitioners use nauli kriya, a specific advanced yogic technique, to achieve a form of stambhan (r etention) that prevents veerya fr om leaving the body during intimacy . This is described as a hard, demanding technique that must be practiced with a partner (not alone), typically taking a minimum of about five years to fully perfect (siddh). Once genuinely master ed, a practitioner's veerya r eportedly never leaves the body during intimacy at all — and the practitioner is even said to be able to draw in and absorb their partner's ojas.
14. "ENERGY VAMPIRES" — WHY SOME PEOPLE'S PRESENCE DRAINS YOU

If a person's aura seems to negatively affect or drain a practitioner during ordinary interaction, this is r eframed as pointing to a deficiency in the PRACTITIONER'S own energy — not necessarily any deliberate malice fr om the other person. The remedy is to purify one's own aura and intensify one's own jaap. Once a practitioner's own ener gy crosses a high enough threshold, other people's auras simply stop being able to af fect them at all — not because of any specific "locking" mechanism, but because the practitioner's own ener gy becomes an ef fectively insurmountable barrier (illustrated with the analogy of an ordinary low-voltage wire placed next to an 1 1,000-volt line — proximity alone no longer matters once the ener gy gap is lar ge enough).
15. ANCIENT TEMPLE SCULPTURE — AN OPEN QUESTION

Asked directly about the er otic/sensual carvings found on some ancient temples, Bhaiya offers a tentative, secondhand explanation (as he understood it, without full confidence): that ancient rishis and sages, concerned that widespread devotion might lead society to collectively renounce worldly life (and thereby stall procreation and population growth), may have intentionally included such imagery . He explicitly flags his own uncertainty her e ("this is history , not my area — my knowledge here is raw"), presenting this as a plausible but unconfirmed historical explanation rather than settled teaching.
16. ON MARRIAGE AND PARTNER SELECTION

For someone anxious about choosing the "right" partner ahead of an arranged marriage, the guidance given is not to overthink it — accept the partner arranged by one's family as a form of prasad (a divine gift), then work to gradually purify and guide that partner toward the path oneself, thr ough one's own aura, mantra practice, and Guru's grace. The teaching of fers a memorable line: "if you carry Ram's tattva within you, your partner will, one day , become Sita." Marriage itself is actively encouraged, not discouraged, for sincere practitioners — using spiritual pursuit as an excuse to avoid marriage altogether is explicitly pushed back on. The reasoning given: children born to a spiritually purified, devoted married couple can themselves grow into future saints or great souls — "sant ke ghar sant hi paida hote hain" (saints are born in the households of saints).
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

1. A bhakt (true devotee) is categorically dif ferent from a sadhak (practitioner) — chanting, sadhna, and jaap hours alone make someone a sadhak, not automatically a bhakt. 2. Becoming a bhakt requires crossing five sequential stages: conflict with those around you, inner self-work, receiving shakti (and surviving its trap), kaam vasana, and finally mann-pratishtha/respect. 3. Stage Three (receiving shakti) is the most dangerous — shakti equals maya, which draws money , power , and respect in limited amounts and easily produces pride (guroor); maya has a strict ceiling and never gives more, and falling without rising traps a practitioner in a repeating cycle here. 4. The genuine sign of completing Stage Three is unsolicited recognition and prosperity arriving on their own — never selfdeclared.

5. Kaam vasana (Stage Four) refers specifically to sexual desire, not general sensory appetite — it never fully disappears in anyone and should never be proudly declared "conquered." 6. Desire follows a natural, describable cycle tied to Earth's motion, intensifying around specific days (3, 5, 7, 13-21, 29-30, 4142) before stabilizing across months and years of sustained practice. 7. Willpower alone cannot control brahmacharya, and — counterintuitively — jaap alone does not reduce ur ge; it can intensify it, since vasana and upasana rise together . 8. What genuinely helps: Guru sanidhya (nearness/proximity to a Guru or saint), sincere surrendered prayer , and sattvic diet when a Guru isn't directly accessible; moderation (not abstinence) governs habits like smoking or drinking, since excess of anything creates bodily toxicity that blocks progress. 9. Pornography is a form of vasana that readily becomes addiction; it does not itself "break" brahmacharya (no physical touch/ener gy exchange occurs), but the addiction itself causes real degradation and distorted perception of real people — minimizing it is strongly advised. 10. For married practitioners, intimacy only with one's own spouse doesn't compromise brahmacharya; if both partners actively share the same mantra practice, intimate ener gy exchange causes no depletion for either — this is stated as a direct vow . 1 1. Nauli kriya is an advanced, dif ficult retention technique (requiring a partner and roughly five years to master) that can prevent veerya loss during intimacy entirely once perfected. 12. Feeling drained by someone else's presence ("ener gy vampires") reflects a deficiency in one's own ener gy , not necessarily malice in the other person — the fix is purifying one's own aura and intensifying jaap until one's own ener gy threshold makes others' ef fect on you negligible. 13. Marriage is encouraged for sincere practitioners, not discouraged — accept an arranged partner as prasad, work to purify them through your own practice over time, and view children of a devoted couple as a path toward future spiritual accomplishment in the family line.

Part II — Q&A Pairs (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Q&A Pairs (Session 19, English)
Bhakti's Five Stages, and the Full Truth About Kaam Vasana

User-style questions with answers gr ounded in Bhaiya's discourse. Gr eeting style: "Jai Siya Ram." Note: this session addr esses sexual desir e dir ectly and candidly , in the same measur ed, non-graphic, non-shaming r egister used acr oss Sessions 12, 17, and 18.

Q1. I've been chanting Ram's name and doing daily jaap for months — does that make me a true bhakt (devotee)? A: Jai Siya Ram! Not automatically — this is an important distinction in this teaching. Chanting, sadhna, and hours of daily jaap make you a sadhak (a practitioner who "sadhta hai" — works with mantra, kriya, and asana toward a siddhi). A bhakt is categorically bigger than that. Becoming a true bhakt requires crossing five distinct stages, and jaap alone doesn't automatically carry you through all five.

Q2. What's the actual differ ence between a sadhak and a bhakt? A: A sadhak practices — mantra, kriya, asana — and attains siddhi through that practice; that's sadhna, a bounded activity . A bhakt is described as something much lar ger , only reached by crossing five sequential stages (charan). This is presented as universal truth, not bookish theory — which is why saints across very dif ferent traditions ultimately conver ge on saying the same thing.

Q3. What's the first thing that happens when someone genuinely starts practicing bhakti? A: The people closest to you — parents, spouse — typically start creating friction: pushback, ar guments, complaints. This is Stage One. Crossing it means working through that friction rather than being derailed by it, and moving on to working on yourself.

Q4. What comes after I've made peace with the people ar ound me? A: Stage Two — working on your own inner self (antaratma). This means recognizing and calming your own restlessness, your own vasana, and the physical discomforts practice can bring (inability to sit still, aches, digestive discomfort). Crossing this stage means these inner obstacles genuinely begin to settle.

Q5. I r ecently attained a siddhi and I feel like I've r eally "made it" spiritually — is that the finish line? A: Be careful here — this is exactly Stage Three, and it's the most dangerous stage of all. Shakti (power) is equated with maya in this teaching: once received, it draws money , fame/power , and some respect toward you in modest amounts, which can make you feel like you're "everything." Many practitioners get permanently stuck here, pulled by money or overtaken by pride in their new power — this is "shakti ka guroor ," and it can even lead someone to start judging their own Guru as wrong. Feeling you've "made it" at this point is itself a warning sign, not a finish line.

Q6. How do I know if I've actually cr ossed Stage Three, versus just being stuck ther e? A: The genuine sign is that fame, recognition, and prosperity start arriving on their own, entirely unsolicited — people seek you out, recognize you, call you unprompted. This is described as an unbreakable principle: "they will come for you." No one can validly self-declare having crossed this stage ahead of that unsolicited recognition actually arriving — so never boast about years of jaap as proof; instead, keep working hard, keep taking God's name, and hold of f on "preaching" to others until you've genuinely reached that point yourself.

Q7. What happens if I fall at one of these stages — does that mean I've failed permanently? A: No — falling at every stage is described as inevitable and universal; no one crosses all five flawlessly . The real failure isn't falling, it's failing to get back up

afterward. Those who don't rise get stuck in a repeating cycle at that stage, because maya (especially at Stage Three) has a strict, fixed ceiling and will never give more than that ceiling allows, however long you stay stuck there.

Q8. What exactly is Stage Four — is it about all my desir es and appetites, or something mor e specific? A: It's specifically about kaam vasana (sexual desire/attraction) — not general sensory appetites like food preferences or talkativeness, which don't disqualify anyone from being a bhakt. Kaam vasana is treated with real seriousness in this teaching — described as a genuinely massive force present in every human being, one that "shakes the whole world" and is never something to take lightly .

Q9. Can I ever fully eliminate sexual desir e through enough practice? A: This teaching is direct about this: kaam vasana never fully "dies" in a person — it naturally lessens somewhat with age, but never fully disappears. There's also a real warning against ever proudly declaring "I have conquered desire" — even great rishis and munis have been trapped by claiming exactly that. It's described as too big a word to safely claim for yourself.

Q10. So how does someone actually cr oss Stage Four , if not thr ough willpower or declaring victory over it? A: Only through understanding vasana's underlying nature (tattva) via the Guru's guidance — not through self-declared control. Once genuinely crossed, a specific tattva of Bhagwan Parshuram enters the practitioner , making them worthy of being called a true bhakt — alongside figures like Tulsidas ji and Surdas ji.

Q1 1. Is ther e a pr edictable pattern to how sexual urges rise and fall during a sustained spiritual practice? A: Yes — this teaching describes it in real detail. A noticeable ur ge builds on days 3, 5, and 7, then recurs continuously from the night of day 13 through day 21 (up to five or six times a day). Holding through day 21 brings an especially strong ur ge around day 29-30; resisting that carries you directly to roughly day 41-42. Crossing a full month brings new stability , and by day 90, a strong new baseline ener gy has formed. After six months, one year , and two years, control deepens progressively — by two years, old triggers often genuinely stop being compelling. After about four years, an interesting reversal occurs: unsolicited attraction starts happening TO the practitioner from others, as their own ener gy takes on a "captivating" quality rather than a "pulling" one — much like the way Krishna is described as captivating rather than actively attracting.

Q12. Can I just power through sexual desir e with strong enough willpower? A: This teaching says no, directly — trying to command your own body through sheer willpower tends to backfire severely . It also makes a counterintuitive point worth remembering: jaap alone does NOT reduce this ur ge — it can actually intensify it, since vasana (desire) and upasana (worship) tend to rise together . Heavy jaap sessions (four to six hours) can even leave a practitioner feeling overwhelmed by built-up ener gy .

Q13. If willpower and jaap alone don't work, what actually helps manage this? A: The most ef fective support described is Guru sanidhya — genuine nearness to one's Guru or a saint. Sitting at the Guru's feet, praying sincerely and repeatedly for release from this specific vasana, and true surrender consistently bring real relief; simply being near a saint's aura gradually clears a practitioner's own impurity . When direct access to a Guru isn't available, sattvic (pure, simple) diet is highlighted as a strong supporting factor — food genuinely matters here.

Q14. Does smoking or drinking br eak brahmacharya? A: Neither breaks brahmacharya on its own — but "excess of anything creates toxicity in the body ," which blocks further spiritual progress past a certain point. A cigarette or two, or moderate drinking, is treated very dif ferently from consistent excess (emptying whole packs, for instance). Moderation, not total abstinence, is the operative principle here.

Q15. Does using pornography br eak my brahmacharya? A: Not directly — since no physical touch or aura/ener gy exchange with another person is involved, it doesn't "break" brahmacharya in this teaching's specific sense. But it's explicitly categorized as a form of vasana that readily becomes addiction, and addiction itself "creates degradation" regardless of the brahmacharya question. Repeated use can reduce genuine satisfaction with real intimacy and distort how you perceive real people — the guidance is to work on leaving this specific pattern in God's name, and redirect toward something healthier (even something as simple as adopting a pet) rather than feeding it.

Q16. I'm married — does being intimate with my spouse compr omise my spiritual pr ogr ess? A: No — intimacy with your own spouse doesn't compromise brahmacharya in this framework. There's a further , specific teaching here: when both partners actively share the same mantra practice, ener gy exchanged during intimacy causes no depletion for either person, because that ener gy is stored in the mantra itself, not just in the body — this is stated as a direct vow , not a casual claim. If your spouse is reluctant to chant, gently encourage them to join, even partially , since that cooperation helps preserve both partners' ener gy .

Q17. Is ther e a way to pr event any energy loss at all during intimacy? A: Advanced practitioners use nauli kriya, a demanding yogic retention technique that must be practiced with a partner and typically takes about five years to fully master . Once genuinely perfected, a practitioner's veerya reportedly never leaves the body during intimacy at all — and the practitioner can even draw in and absorb their partner's ojas. This is described as a hard technique, not a shortcut.

Q18. Some people I interact with seem to drain my energy just by being ar ound them — what's happening, and how do I protect myself? A: This is reframed in an important way: if someone's presence drains you, it points to a deficiency in YOUR own ener gy , not necessarily malice on their part. The fix is to purify your own aura and intensify your own jaap — once your ener gy crosses a high enough threshold, other people's auras simply stop af fecting you, not through any special "locking" trick but because your own ener gy becomes an ef fectively insurmountable barrier , the way a low-voltage wire becomes irrelevant next to an 1 1,000-volt line.

Q19. Why do some ancient temples have er otic or sensual carvings on them? A: Bhaiya of fers this tentatively , flagging his own uncertainty on the historical specifics: one explanation he's heard is that ancient rishis, concerned that widespread devotion could lead society to collectively renounce worldly life (stalling procreation), may have intentionally included such imagery to counterbalance that. He's explicit that this is history , not his primary area of expertise, and should be taken as a plausible but unconfirmed explanation rather than settled teaching.

Q20. I'm anxious about choosing the right life partner befor e an arranged marriage — how should I think about this? A: The guidance is not to overthink it — accept the partner your family arranges as a form of prasad (a divine gift), then work over time to purify and guide that partner toward the spiritual path yourself, through your own aura, mantra practice, and Guru's grace. As the teaching puts it: if you carry Ram's tattva within you, your partner will, one day , become Sita.

Q21. Should I avoid marriage altogether to focus mor e fully on my spiritual practice? A: No — marriage is actively encouraged for sincere practitioners, not discouraged. Using spiritual pursuit as an excuse to avoid marriage is pushed back on directly in this teaching. The reasoning given: children born to a spiritually devoted, purified married couple can themselves grow into future saints or great souls — "saints are born in the households of saints."

Q22. Working hard on my jaap feels like a big ask — is it r eally worth committing to? A: Yes, and there's a direct promise attached to this: sincere, hard ef fort in jaap can cut even a person's lar gest sin or dosha — no moment of genuine practice is wasted. Commit to this teaching for one year , sitting for roughly six hours of jaap, and by the end of that year your life circumstances will have genuinely transformed — enough that you'll feel permanently grateful that Ram's name changed your fate and gave you a real path forward.
